name: ThinkWatchProject/ThinkWatch
summary: An AI gateway whose most unusual feature is refusing to report a cost it cannot price, instead of quietly calling it zero.

agent_relevance.agent_integration_path: Strong on paper, unexercised in practice. The product is itself an MCP gateway with per-user OAuth and tokens and tool-level RBAC, exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint that agents can target directly, and names Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Continue, Cline, opencode and Zed plus the OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini SDKs as supported clients. An agent integrates by pointing at one gateway URL with a scoped key. We could not verify any of this behaviourally: the captured surface demonstrated it only with sample data.

hlido_opinion.headline: An AI gateway whose most unusual feature is refusing to report a cost it cannot price, instead of quietly calling it zero.
hlido_opinion.body: Gateways that route model traffic are now a crowded category, and almost all of them claim cost visibility. ThinkWatch is notable for stating the limits of its own measurement. Tokens are priced per model, usage without a known price is reported as unknown rather than folded into a total, estimated amounts are marked as estimates, and requests without a price are counted separately rather than as zero. That is a small amount of copy carrying a large amount of integrity: an accounting surface that cannot say what it does not know is far more useful to a team doing chargeback than one that always produces a confident number. The rest of the product is a competent two-shape offering - a local desktop gateway for an individual developer on macOS, Windows and Linux, and a self-hosted server for an organisation - with the enterprise side covering per-user OAuth on MCP, tool-level RBAC, five roles with any OIDC provider, sliding-window request and token limits, spending budgets per user, key or role, and audit logs forwardable to a SIEM. The relay-protection framing is the second thing worth noting: credentials can be replaced before a request leaves so a relay never holds them, dangerous tool calls injected into an answer can be cut off before the client runs them, and MCP servers, skills and hooks are themselves scanned. Plugins run in a sandbox, see placeholders instead of keys, and every change they make is recorded. The weakness is evidential: the console preview is explicitly sample data, the request trace shows bracketed illustrative values, and nothing on the surface is a demonstration a reader could reproduce.

tier_rationale: STEADY (75) because the product addresses a real and specific operational need, the enterprise control surface is enumerated concretely rather than gestured at, versions are published with a changelog, and the cost-accounting honesty - unknown prices reported as unknown, estimates marked, unpriced requests counted separately - is a genuine differentiator in a category that routinely over-claims. Not VITAL because every visible demonstration is labelled sample or illustrative, there is no reproducible demo or benchmark a reader could run, the public surface offered no clear primary call to action when captured, and no operating history or third-party deployment is evidenced - so the strongest claims rest on the vendor's own description of behaviour we could not exercise.
what_it_does_well: States the limits of its own cost measurement: unknown prices are reported as unknown, estimates are marked, and unpriced requests are counted separately rather than as zero

Enumerates the enterprise control surface concretely - per-user OAuth on MCP, tool-level RBAC, five roles with any OIDC provider, sliding-window limits, per-user and per-key budgets, SIEM-forwardable audit logs

Treats the relay itself as untrusted: credentials can be substituted before a request leaves, injected high-risk tool calls can be cut off before the client runs them, and MCP servers, skills and hooks are scanned
Runs plugins in a sandbox that sees placeholders rather than keys, and records every change a plugin makes
Ships two honest shapes for two different buyers - a local desktop gateway for an individual developer and a self-hosted server for an organisation - rather than one product stretched across both
Publishes explicit version numbers and a changelog (Enterprise 3.10.0, Lite 2026.10.34) with per-platform build sizes
what_it_fails_at: Every demonstration on the surface is labelled sample data or illustrative, including the console preview and the request trace with bracketed values
No reproducible demo, trial trace or benchmark a reader could run themselves
No pricing figures were visible on the captured surface beyond the existence of a pricing page
No operating history, named deployment or third-party validation is evidenced
The captured homepage offered no single clear primary action, splitting the reader between two products immediately
best_for: Teams that need per-user attribution and chargeback for model spend and cannot accept a total that silently includes guesses
Organisations required to self-host the gateway handling model and MCP traffic rather than route it through a vendor
Security teams that treat the model relay as untrusted and want credential substitution and tool-call inspection at the boundary
Individual developers wanting one local endpoint for Claude Code, Codex and similar clients with provider switching behind it
not_recommended_for: Buyers who need to see the product working before committing, since every visible trace and dashboard is sample data
Teams wanting a fully managed hosted gateway - the offering is a local app or a self-hosted server
Anyone needing published price-performance or latency figures for the routing layer
Organisations that require a third-party reference deployment before adopting infrastructure on the credential path
red_flags: Every capability demonstration is explicitly sample or illustrative data, so nothing on the public surface independently evidences that the described routing, metering and redaction behave as stated
The product sits directly on the credential path and scans MCP servers, skills and hooks, yet no security audit, disclosure policy or third-party review is referenced

compared_to.verdict_diff: OpenRouter is a hosted multi-model endpoint; ThinkWatch is a gateway you run yourself with identity, RBAC and audit on top. Choose OpenRouter to avoid operating anything; choose ThinkWatch when the traffic and the audit log must stay inside your perimeter.

Helicone centres on observability and analytics for model calls; ThinkWatch centres on being an enforcement point - auth, RBAC, budgets, redaction - with accounting attached, and is explicit about not pricing what it cannot price. Choose Helicone for analytics depth; choose ThinkWatch when requests must be blocked or rewritten, not just measured.

Langfuse instruments and traces LLM applications for developers; ThinkWatch sits in the network path as a gateway for an organisation. They are complementary more often than competing - Langfuse answers why an application behaved as it did, ThinkWatch answers who was allowed to spend what.

evidence_urls.claim: Routes, inspects and meters model requests and MCP tool calls, as a self-hosted server or a desktop app
Usage without a known price is reported as unknown, estimates are marked, and unpriced requests are counted separately rather than as zero
Secrets are redacted before requests reach an upstream and high-risk tool calls are flagged
Enterprise provides per-user OAuth on MCP, tool-level RBAC, five roles with any OIDC provider, sliding-window limits and SIEM-forwardable audit logs
The console preview and request trace are labelled sample data with bracketed illustrative values
